labor.title: AI & Jobs
labor.intro: How many workers worldwide are affected by AI? This overview shows three layers: what studies consider possible (theory), what companies worldwide plan (plan), and what has been concretely reported so far (reality). Theory and plan say a lot — reality is very unevenly distributed.
labor.section.theory: Potential analysis — what studies consider possible
labor.section.reality: Reality — what has been concretely reported so far
labor.plan.source: WEF Future of Jobs Survey 2025 — over 1,000 employers, 14M workers, 22 industries, 55 economies.
labor.plan.item1: plan workforce reduction in AI-automatable areas
labor.plan.item3: plan internal redeployment rather than layoffs
labor.plan.note: Employers' own expectations — plan, not realized outcome.
labor.reality.note: Curated to best knowledge from journalistic sources. Counter includes only cases with explicit AI attribution (strength 4–5 of 5). Global loss trackers do not yet exist — we collect cases individually and rely on contributions.
laborMap.title: AI & Jobs · Map
laborMap.intro: Concretely reported AI-driven workforce changes per country. Marker size scales with the number of reported positions. Click a marker to see that country's cases in the detail panel.
laborMap.aria: World map with reported AI-driven workforce changes per country
laborMap.selectCountry: Click a marker to see the country's cases.
labor.substitutionDesc: Share of the global workforce whose tasks AI systems could replace — not necessarily will.
labor.augmentationDesc: Share of the global workforce whose tasks AI systems could augment or make more productive — not replace.
labor.caveatBody: Substitution and augmentation are not a balance sheet. Where AI replaces jobs, far fewer new jobs are typically created to build, maintain and operate the AI itself — the two sides are not equal in size. We therefore do not show a net. The sources measure contact with AI, not the real effect on employment.

privacy.crowdsourcing.title: 8. Crowdsourcing submissions (incidents, AI workforce changes)
privacy.crowdsourcing.intro: AIStrikeMap allows users to submit AI-related incidents and concretely reported workforce changes via GitHub issue templates. The following data is collected:
privacy.crowdsourcing.public: Public (visible in the repository): the substantive content (company, country, date, headcount, sources, AI quote, context) — published as a JSON file in the public repository after editorial review.
privacy.crowdsourcing.private: Private (internal, not public): optional real name and contact email of the submitter — kept exclusively in internal editorial storage (separate, non-public system) and used only for follow-up questions for quality assurance.
privacy.crowdsourcing.anonymous: Anonymous submissions are possible, but we cannot then ask follow-up questions — the case may be discarded without further clarification.
privacy.crowdsourcing.legal: Legal basis: legitimate interest in quality assurance and source verification (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR). Purpose: follow-up on submissions, source clarification, building relationships with informants. Recipients: only the editorial team (Ironhark / Kommuniziere in), no transfer to third parties. Retention: up to 5 years after last activity, then deletion.
privacy.crowdsourcing.review: Pre-publication review: every submission is editorially reviewed before publication. Content with unsupported factual claims, discrediting risk to companies or persons, or lacking source robustness is rejected or anonymised. Concept and workflow are publicly documented in recht-crowdsourcing.md.
privacy.crowdsourcing.rights: Access and deletion rights (see section 7 above) also apply to crowdsourcing submissions. Requests to the contact address listed in the imprint.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: This page describes the scientific and editorial principles by which AIStrikeMap records, evaluates and presents incidents.
methodology.verification.title: 4-Stage verification model
methodology.verification.intro: Every incident undergoes a four-stage verification procedure. The current stage is transparently displayed in the map view.
methodology.verification.l1:
Stage 1 — Reported
An incident has been identified from a source or reported by users. At least one primary or secondary source exists. No editorial review has taken place. The entry is marked as unverified.
methodology.verification.l2:
Stage 2 — Confirmed
At least two independent sources confirm the incident. Basic facts (location, time, actors involved) are plausible. Obvious false reports and duplicates have been sorted out.
methodology.verification.l3:
Stage 3 — Verified
Detailed review by the editorial team. Source quality assessed, contradictions documented, context researched. The incident is supported by reliable sources and classified in the taxonomy.
methodology.verification.l4:
Stage 4 — Analysed
Full investigation including reverse timeline, contextualisation within industry trends and connection to related incidents. Systemic causes are identified. Only selected incidents reach this stage.
methodology.timeline.title: Reverse timeline concept
methodology.timeline.intro: Classical reporting asks: What happened? The reverse timeline additionally asks: Why could it happen? For this, each analysed incident is unwound along four levels:
methodology.timeline.infrastructure:
Infrastructure
What technical infrastructure (models, training data, deployment pipelines) underlies the incident? Who developed and operated it?
methodology.timeline.doctrine:
Doctrine
What corporate policies, regulatory frameworks or missing governance structures enabled or facilitated the incident?
methodology.timeline.event:
Event
What exactly happened? Chronological reconstruction of the incident with sources, timestamps and actors involved.
methodology.timeline.consequences:
Consequences
What impact did the incident have? Affected persons, regulatory reactions, technical corrections, public debate.
methodology.timeline.outro: Through this approach, systemic patterns become visible that remain hidden when individual incidents are viewed in isolation.
methodology.taxonomy.title: Taxonomy of incident types
methodology.taxonomy.intro: Incidents are classified by their primary type of harm. An incident may be assigned to multiple categories.
methodology.taxonomy.surveillance: Surveillance — Use of AI for mass surveillance or targeted observation
methodology.taxonomy.predictivePolicing: Predictive Policing — Algorithmic prediction of crime and preventive policing
methodology.taxonomy.autonomousWeapons: Autonomous Weapons — AI-controlled weapons systems and autonomous combat means
methodology.taxonomy.bias: Discrimination / Bias — Systematic disadvantage of certain groups through AI systems
methodology.taxonomy.deepfakes: Deepfakes / Disinformation — AI-generated false information, synthetic media, manipulation campaigns
methodology.taxonomy.dataAbuse: Data abuse — Unauthorised data collection, data leaks, violations of privacy through AI
methodology.taxonomy.military: Military AI use — Use of AI in military decision chains and operations
methodology.taxonomy.facialRecognition: Facial recognition — Biometric identification and mass capture of faces
methodology.taxonomy.censorship: Censorship / Content control — AI-supported suppression of information and opinions
methodology.taxonomy.laborExploitation: AI labor exploitation — Exploitation of annotation work, content moderation under inhumane conditions
methodology.taxonomy.politicalPressure: Political pressure on AI safety — Influence on safety standards and responsible AI development
methodology.severity.title: Severity scale
methodology.severity.intro: Each incident receives a severity rating from 1 to 5. The scale considers extent, reversibility and number of those affected.
methodology.severity.l1Desc: Ethical concerns, no immediate danger. Limited impact, easily reversible, few affected.
methodology.severity.l2Desc: Fundamental rights potentially affected. Measurable impact on a limited group, mostly reversible.
methodology.severity.l3Desc: Demonstrated violation of fundamental rights. Significant impact on a larger group, partially irreversible.
methodology.severity.l4Desc: Physical or existential threat. Serious impact, largely irreversible, many affected.
methodology.severity.l5Desc: Immediate danger to life and limb. Life-threatening impact, irreversible, potentially systemic.
methodology.sources.title: Source standards
methodology.sources.intro: The following source requirements apply for inclusion and evaluation of incidents:
methodology.sources.primary: Primary sources preferred — court documents, official reports, technical audits, statements from those affected
methodology.sources.secondary: Secondary sources — reporting from established media, reports from NGOs and research institutions
methodology.sources.twoIndependent: At least two independent sources for stage 2 and higher
methodology.sources.archival: Archiving — All cited sources are archived where possible (Wayback Machine, local copies)
methodology.sources.transparentGaps: Transparent gaps — Missing or contradictory information is openly documented, not glossed over
methodology.sources.noAnonymous: No anonymous single sources — Anonymous tips are only accepted if supported by at least one publicly accessible source
transparency.title: Transparency
transparency.intro: AIStrikeMap commits to full disclosure of the tools, methods and possible conflicts of interest used. This page documents how the project operates and where its limits lie.
transparency.tools.title: Tools used
transparency.tools.claudeCode: Claude Code (Anthropic) — Technical development: code generation, architecture, debugging
transparency.tools.claude: Claude (Anthropic) — Research support: source search, summarisation, fact-checking
transparency.aiDisclosure.title: AI disclosure
transparency.aiDisclosure.p1: Technical implementation through AI (Claude Code). Editorial curation and verification by [Name].
transparency.aiDisclosure.p2: Specifically: The source code of this website was written with AI support. All editorial entries — incident descriptions, source references, categorisations and assessments — are reviewed and approved by humans. AI-generated suggestions are flagged as such until they are verified by a human.
transparency.conflict.title: Conflict of interest disclosure
transparency.conflict.p1: This project was developed with tools from Anthropic. To counteract a potential conflict of interest, incidents involving Anthropic products are presented deliberately prominently and are not played down. We regard self-critical scrutiny as a quality criterion.
transparency.conflict.p2: Should users notice an unbalanced presentation of Anthropic-related incidents, we ask for a report via the contact address listed in the imprint.
transparency.funding.title: Funding
transparency.funding.intro: AIStrikeMap is an independent, non-commercial project. Funding is provided exclusively through transparent channels:
transparency.funding.openCollective: Open Collective Europe — [placeholder link]
transparency.funding.outro: There are no funding relationships with AI companies, governments or arms companies. All donations are publicly documented.
transparency.code.title: Source code
transparency.code.text: The entire source code is publicly available: GitHub repository. The code is licensed under the AGPL-3.0 license.
transparency.limits.title: Limits of the platform
transparency.limits.intro: AIStrikeMap cannot and does not want to provide the following:
transparency.limits.completeness: Completeness — We make no claim to a complete record of all AI-related incidents worldwide. Regional coverage varies considerably.
transparency.limits.realtime: Real-time reporting — Entries go through a multi-stage verification process. It may take weeks before an incident is included.
transparency.limits.legal: Legal assessment — The platform documents incidents but does not undertake a legal classification.
transparency.limits.causality: Proof of causality — We document correlations and plausible connections, but in many cases cannot demonstrate clear causality.
transparency.limits.globalSouth: Global South — Due to language barriers and limited access to local sources, incidents outside the English- and German-speaking world are underrepresented. We are actively working to improve this.
privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.responsible.title: 1. Data controller
privacy.responsible.text: The data controller within the meaning of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the person named in the imprint.
privacy.collection.title: 2. Collection and processing of personal data
privacy.collection.intro: This website is provided via GitHub Pages. When the website is accessed, the hosting provider (GitHub, Inc.) automatically records the following data in server log files:
privacy.collection.ip: IP address of the accessing device
privacy.collection.ua: User agent (browser and operating system information)
privacy.collection.outro: This data is processed by GitHub. We ourselves have no access to these server log files. Further information can be found in GitHub's privacy policy.
privacy.purpose.title: 3. Purpose of data processing
privacy.purpose.text: The processing of server log data is technically necessary for providing and securing the website.
privacy.legalBasis.title: 4. Legal basis
privacy.legalBasis.text: Processing is carried out on the basis of Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest). Our legitimate interest lies in the technical provision and security of the website.
privacy.cookies.title: 5. Cookies and tracking
privacy.cookies.text: This website uses no cookies and employs no tracking. No analysis or advertising services are used.
privacy.externalServices.title: 6. External services
privacy.externalServices.intro: To display the interactive map and user interface, the following external services are embedded:
privacy.externalServices.unpkgText: The JavaScript library Leaflet is loaded via the Content Delivery Network unpkg.com. When accessed, your IP address is transmitted to the CDN operator. This is technically necessary for the map function. Further information: unpkg.com.
privacy.externalServices.cartoText: The map display uses tiles from CARTO (basemaps.cartocdn.com), which are based on OpenStreetMap data. When loading the map sections, your IP address is transmitted to CARTO servers. Use is in accordance with the CARTO privacy policy and the OpenStreetMap Foundation privacy policy.
privacy.externalServices.outro: The legal basis for embedding external services is likewise Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in a functional map display).
privacy.rights.title: 7. Your rights (data subject rights)
privacy.rights.intro: You have the following rights under the GDPR:
privacy.rights.access: Right of access (Art. 15 GDPR) — right to obtain information about your processed data
privacy.rights.rectification: Right to rectification (Art. 16 GDPR) — right to correction of inaccurate data
privacy.rights.deletion: Right to erasure (Art. 17 GDPR) — right to deletion of your data
privacy.rights.restriction: Restriction of processing (Art. 18 GDPR) — right to restriction of data processing
privacy.rights.portability: Data portability (Art. 20 GDPR) — right to transfer your data
privacy.rights.objection: Right to object (Art. 21 GDPR) — right to object to the processing
privacy.rights.contact: To exercise your rights, please contact the address provided in the imprint.
privacy.rights.complaint: In addition, you have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority (Art. 77 GDPR).
